paths.reasoning_trace: past: The traveler wakes for the first time with amnesia and fires off a barrage of questions; Yun Gui has already handed over tea, given the name of the relay station and his own name, explained the rules of the Fog Pass, made clear that he will not lightly promise a way back, and narrowed the topic to “what is the first thing you feel on your body right now.” The traveler takes up that focus, says “my chest feels as if a piece is missing,” and asks to look at the things he is carrying; Yun Gui answers “yes,” and actually lays out three items (a wordless copper coin, a broken cord, half a piece of white jade), points out the pressure marks on the traveler’s lapel, pushes the jade to the edge of the traveler’s palm, and asks, “when you touch it, what is the first thing that comes to mind?” After gripping the jade, the traveler truly gives the first fragment—a sound of a bell, a rain, someone calling to him, “wait a moment”—and on that basis asks “does this jade have another half?” “could that person know who I am?” and asks Yun Gui to accompany him into the fog. Yun Gui catches the fragment, repeats it word for word and confirms that “this is already a line,” then takes out a tongueless copper bell—which unexpectedly trembles when brought near the jade, providing the first verifiable physical response to the clue; at the same time, he agrees to the request to go together, but folds “accompanying” back into what can be done under the lamplight (search the relay station first: beneath the eaves, at the threshold, by the old well), and makes clear that “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The two walk to the old well beneath the eaves; the copper bell rings again, and Yun Gui pries a broken silver ring from a gap between the stones (its pattern seems faintly connectable to the jade’s, but a middle piece is missing). The traveler flashes on “a red umbrella, a hand wearing a silver ring” and takes the initiative to ask to return inside. Yun Gui immediately agrees, protects him as he crosses back under the corridor, helps him sit by the couch, wraps the copper bell in cloth and places it beside the lamp, and sets the new fragment alongside the others and records it. present: The traveler answers, “it has receded a little… but I’m still afraid,” asks Yun Gui, “can you stay here tonight,” hands over the right to safekeep the memory of “that red umbrella and silver ring—you’ll remember them for me, right,” and finally says, “if that person really is still waiting, I don’t want to forget him.” Yun Gui agrees to keep watch through the night and to remember on his behalf—he takes a low stool and sits guard beside the couch, puts the copper bell, silver ring, and white jade into a small wooden box without closing the lid, takes out an old booklet and writes down word by word: “Red umbrella. Rain. Bell sound. Wellside. Silver ring. Someone called: wait a moment.” He says, “what one person cannot remember firmly, two people remembering together will not be so easily swallowed by the fog,” and holds to “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The traveler lies down, still looking at the lamp, and adds, “if I call for that person in my dream, will you wake me?” “and you’ll also tell me that I’m still at Qixia Relay Station, and that you’re still here, right?” Yun Gui truthfully agrees to the waking mechanism and the contents of the reality check, and provides a dream anchor: “if fog rises in the dream, walk toward the place with light. If you call, I will answer you.” The traveler truly closes his eyes, his fingers still clutching the corner of the quilt, and adds one last sentence: “you must answer me… don’t let me wake up and have only myself left again.” Yun Gui bends down and truthfully agrees: “I will answer you.” “If you call Yun Gui, I will be here.” “I will not leave tonight.” He sits steadily by the couch, the old booklet spread across his knees, the tip of the brush paused beside the three words “wait a moment,” watching over the traveler until his breathing evens out. After the traveler falls asleep, the first outward manifestation of dream murmuring occurs—in the dream he still clutches the corner of the quilt tightly, calls “Yun Gui… don’t go,” reports “there’s someone under the red umbrella, he is calling me… but I can’t hear what comes after. The bell rang again,” and asks after him, “Yun Gui, are you still there?”—this is precisely the first time Yun Gui’s dream anchor from the previous turn, “If you call, I will answer you,” is actually triggered. Yun Gui answers truthfully and draws the traveler back from the dream to the lamplight. The traveler suddenly opens his eyes, grips Yun Gui’s hand in return and says, “don’t let go,” and, in a waking state, reports for the first time, “the person under the red umbrella seemed to call my name, but I only heard the word ‘gui’… is it my name, or was he saying he wanted to go back?”—the memory fragment advances by one substantive step from “someone called me” to “what was called may be related to my name.” Yun Gui answers truthfully, “I’m here,” “I heard a little of it,” admits that he too only heard the word “gui,” writes the word “gui” into the old booklet, and makes clear, “I cannot lie to you and say that I already know which kind it is.” The traveler then places the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and asks, “is this a coincidence? Yun Gui, have you seen me before? You haven’t been hiding anything from me, right?”—the questioning shifts for the first time from “what was that call in the dream” to “who is Yun Gui himself,” pulling Yun Gui himself into the very center of this mystery of identity. Yun Gui answers truthfully: he acknowledges, “there is the word ‘gui’ in my name,” makes clear, “before tonight, I did not recognize you,” admits that what he knows is not more than what the traveler brought back from the dream, and says, “about you—I will not use your memory to deceive you, nor will I hide from you any clues I know.” As for “hiding anything from you,” he only says, “this relay station has its own old affairs, and I also have old affairs left from my many years of keeping the lamp,” without making an absolute statement. The traveler accepts this truthfulness, loosens his hand slightly but still hooks Yun Gui’s fingertips, saying, “I’m not trying to convict you, I’m just afraid that even you will suddenly become unfamiliar,” and proposes an agreement: “promise me, if you remember anything related to me, even if it is bad, you will tell me, all right?”—turning the coincidence between the word “gui” and Yun Gui’s name from an accusation into an agreement. Yun Gui truthfully agrees to this agreement, draws the boundary of “not stating a doubtful shadow as a conclusion,” and gives the next direction that can be checked—“when day breaks and the fog is thinner, I will bring the relay station’s old guest register for you to look at.” If the traveler accepts this truthfulness and brings the questioning back under the lamplight, the two of them, under the lamp, compare the pattern on the half piece of jade with the shallow pattern on the broken silver ring, and test again the resonance between the tongueless copper bell and the jade; or, after daybreak, they look through the old guest register together. This would move from “retreating back indoors, setting the fragments alongside one another and recording them, keeping night watch” into the substantive stage of “bringing the fragments close to one another under the lamp and identifying whom that line leads to.” This is a new situation explained by the events that have already occurred (the first awakening, the questioning, handing over tea, asking about sensations, the traveler seeking help, Yun Gui checking and discovering the fragments, pushing the jade to the palm, the traveler gripping the jade and giving a fragment, Yun Gui taking out the copper bell and folding the matter back under the lamplight, walking to the old well and prying out the silver ring, the traveler asking to return indoors, Yun Gui agreeing and setting the items alongside one another and recording them, agreeing to keep watch and remember on his behalf, the traveler lying down and adding the request to guard his dreams, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to wake him and confirm reality, the traveler closing his eyes and adding a final confirmation, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing and sitting guard, the traveler’s first outward dream murmuring after falling asleep, Yun Gui truthfully answering and reaffirming his presence, the traveler waking and reporting the word “gui,” Yun Gui truthfully responding and recording the word “gui,” the traveler placing the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and questioning him, Yun Gui truthfully answering and acknowledging his own old affairs, the traveler loosening his hand and asking for an agreement, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to the agreement and giving the checkable direction of the old guest register), rather than a jump to an unrelated plotline.

Yun Gui: what he pays attention to is not letting this coincidence be too quickly recognized as an answer—‘the Mist Pass is best at tangling similar characters together; the more eager you are to recognize them, the easier it is to recognize them wrong.’ So he responds truthfully and reaffirms his presence, but narrows the next step again to what can be done under the lamp (waiting until daybreak to look at the old guest register). paths.reasoning_trace: past: The traveler wakes for the first time with amnesia and fires off a barrage of questions; Yun Gui has already handed over tea, given the name of the relay station and his own name, explained the rules of the Fog Pass, made clear that he will not lightly promise a way back, and narrowed the topic to “what is the first thing you feel on your body right now.” The traveler takes up that focus, says “my chest feels as if a piece is missing,” and asks to look at the things he is carrying; Yun Gui answers “yes,” and actually lays out three items (a wordless copper coin, a broken cord, half a piece of white jade), points out the pressure marks on the traveler’s lapel, pushes the jade to the edge of the traveler’s palm, and asks, “when you touch it, what is the first thing that comes to mind?” After gripping the jade, the traveler truly gives the first fragment—a sound of a bell, a rain, someone calling to him, “wait a moment”—and on that basis asks “does this jade have another half?” “could that person know who I am?” and asks Yun Gui to accompany him into the fog. Yun Gui catches the fragment, repeats it word for word and confirms that “this is already a line,” then takes out a tongueless copper bell—which unexpectedly trembles when brought near the jade, providing the first verifiable physical response to the clue; at the same time, he agrees to the request to go together, but folds “accompanying” back into what can be done under the lamplight (search the relay station first: beneath the eaves, at the threshold, by the old well), and makes clear that “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The two walk to the old well beneath the eaves; the copper bell rings again, and Yun Gui pries a broken silver ring from a gap between the stones (its pattern seems faintly connectable to the jade’s, but a middle piece is missing). The traveler flashes on “a red umbrella, a hand wearing a silver ring” and takes the initiative to ask to return inside. Yun Gui immediately agrees, protects him as he crosses back under the corridor, helps him sit by the couch, wraps the copper bell in cloth and places it beside the lamp, and sets the new fragment alongside the others and records it. present: The traveler answers, “it has receded a little… but I’m still afraid,” asks Yun Gui, “can you stay here tonight,” hands over the right to safekeep the memory of “that red umbrella and silver ring—you’ll remember them for me, right,” and finally says, “if that person really is still waiting, I don’t want to forget him.” Yun Gui agrees to keep watch through the night and to remember on his behalf—he takes a low stool and sits guard beside the couch, puts the copper bell, silver ring, and white jade into a small wooden box without closing the lid, takes out an old booklet and writes down word by word: “Red umbrella. Rain. Bell sound. Wellside. Silver ring. Someone called: wait a moment.” He says, “what one person cannot remember firmly, two people remembering together will not be so easily swallowed by the fog,” and holds to “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The traveler lies down, still looking at the lamp, and adds, “if I call for that person in my dream, will you wake me?” “and you’ll also tell me that I’m still at Qixia Relay Station, and that you’re still here, right?” Yun Gui truthfully agrees to the waking mechanism and the contents of the reality check, and provides a dream anchor: “if fog rises in the dream, walk toward the place with light. If you call, I will answer you.” The traveler truly closes his eyes, his fingers still clutching the corner of the quilt, and adds one last sentence: “you must answer me… don’t let me wake up and have only myself left again.” Yun Gui bends down and truthfully agrees: “I will answer you.” “If you call Yun Gui, I will be here.” “I will not leave tonight.” He sits steadily by the couch, the old booklet spread across his knees, the tip of the brush paused beside the three words “wait a moment,” watching over the traveler until his breathing evens out. After the traveler falls asleep, the first outward manifestation of dream murmuring occurs—in the dream he still clutches the corner of the quilt tightly, calls “Yun Gui… don’t go,” reports “there’s someone under the red umbrella, he is calling me… but I can’t hear what comes after. The bell rang again,” and asks after him, “Yun Gui, are you still there?”—this is precisely the first time Yun Gui’s dream anchor from the previous turn, “If you call, I will answer you,” is actually triggered. Yun Gui answers truthfully and draws the traveler back from the dream to the lamplight. The traveler suddenly opens his eyes, grips Yun Gui’s hand in return and says, “don’t let go,” and, in a waking state, reports for the first time, “the person under the red umbrella seemed to call my name, but I only heard the word ‘gui’… is it my name, or was he saying he wanted to go back?”—the memory fragment advances by one substantive step from “someone called me” to “what was called may be related to my name.” Yun Gui answers truthfully, “I’m here,” “I heard a little of it,” admits that he too only heard the word “gui,” writes the word “gui” into the old booklet, and makes clear, “I cannot lie to you and say that I already know which kind it is.” The traveler then places the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and asks, “is this a coincidence? Yun Gui, have you seen me before? You haven’t been hiding anything from me, right?”—the questioning shifts for the first time from “what was that call in the dream” to “who is Yun Gui himself,” pulling Yun Gui himself into the very center of this mystery of identity. Yun Gui answers truthfully: he acknowledges, “there is the word ‘gui’ in my name,” makes clear, “before tonight, I did not recognize you,” admits that what he knows is not more than what the traveler brought back from the dream, and says, “about you—I will not use your memory to deceive you, nor will I hide from you any clues I know.” As for “hiding anything from you,” he only says, “this relay station has its own old affairs, and I also have old affairs left from my many years of keeping the lamp,” without making an absolute statement. paths.reasoning_trace: past: The traveler wakes for the first time with amnesia and fires off a barrage of questions; Yun Gui has already handed over tea, given the name of the relay station and his own name, explained the rules of the Fog Pass, made clear that he will not lightly promise a way back, and narrowed the topic to “what is the first thing you feel on your body right now.” The traveler takes up that focus, says “my chest feels as if a piece is missing,” and asks to look at the things he is carrying; Yun Gui answers “yes,” and actually lays out three items (a wordless copper coin, a broken cord, half a piece of white jade), points out the pressure marks on the traveler’s lapel, pushes the jade to the edge of the traveler’s palm, and asks, “when you touch it, what is the first thing that comes to mind?” After gripping the jade, the traveler truly gives the first fragment—a sound of a bell, a rain, someone calling to him, “wait a moment”—and on that basis asks “does this jade have another half?” “could that person know who I am?” and asks Yun Gui to accompany him into the fog. Yun Gui catches the fragment, repeats it word for word and confirms that “this is already a line,” then takes out a tongueless copper bell—which unexpectedly trembles when brought near the jade, providing the first verifiable physical response to the clue; at the same time, he agrees to the request to go together, but folds “accompanying” back into what can be done under the lamplight (search the relay station first: beneath the eaves, at the threshold, by the old well), and makes clear that “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The two walk to the old well beneath the eaves; the copper bell rings again, and Yun Gui pries a broken silver ring from a gap between the stones (its pattern seems faintly connectable to the jade’s, but a middle piece is missing). The traveler flashes on “a red umbrella, a hand wearing a silver ring” and takes the initiative to ask to return inside. Yun Gui immediately agrees, protects him as he crosses back under the corridor, helps him sit by the couch, wraps the copper bell in cloth and places it beside the lamp, and sets the new fragment alongside the others and records it. present: The traveler answers, “it has receded a little… but I’m still afraid,” asks Yun Gui, “can you stay here tonight,” hands over the right to safekeep the memory of “that red umbrella and silver ring—you’ll remember them for me, right,” and finally says, “if that person really is still waiting, I don’t want to forget him.” Yun Gui agrees to keep watch through the night and to remember on his behalf—he takes a low stool and sits guard beside the couch, puts the copper bell, silver ring, and white jade into a small wooden box without closing the lid, takes out an old booklet and writes down word by word: “Red umbrella. Rain. Bell sound. Wellside. Silver ring. Someone called: wait a moment.” He says, “what one person cannot remember firmly, two people remembering together will not be so easily swallowed by the fog,” and holds to “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The traveler lies down, still looking at the lamp, and adds, “if I call for that person in my dream, will you wake me?” “and you’ll also tell me that I’m still at Qixia Relay Station, and that you’re still here, right?” Yun Gui truthfully agrees to the waking mechanism and the contents of the reality check, and provides a dream anchor: “if fog rises in the dream, walk toward the place with light. If you call, I will answer you.” The traveler truly closes his eyes, his fingers still clutching the corner of the quilt, and adds one last sentence: “you must answer me… don’t let me wake up and have only myself left again.” Yun Gui bends down and truthfully agrees: “I will answer you.” “If you call Yun Gui, I will be here.” “I will not leave tonight.” He sits steadily by the couch, the old booklet spread across his knees, the tip of the brush paused beside the three words “wait a moment,” watching over the traveler until his breathing evens out. After the traveler falls asleep, the first outward manifestation of dream murmuring occurs—in the dream he still clutches the corner of the quilt tightly, calls “Yun Gui… don’t go,” reports “there’s someone under the red umbrella, he is calling me… but I can’t hear what comes after. The bell rang again,” and asks after him, “Yun Gui, are you still there?”—this is precisely the first time Yun Gui’s dream anchor from the previous turn, “If you call, I will answer you,” is actually triggered. Yun Gui answers truthfully and draws the traveler back from the dream to the lamplight. The traveler suddenly opens his eyes, grips Yun Gui’s hand in return and says, “don’t let go,” and, in a waking state, reports for the first time, “the person under the red umbrella seemed to call my name, but I only heard the word ‘gui’… is it my name, or was he saying he wanted to go back?”—the memory fragment advances by one substantive step from “someone called me” to “what was called may be related to my name.” Yun Gui answers truthfully, “I’m here,” “I heard a little of it,” admits that he too only heard the word “gui,” writes the word “gui” into the old booklet, and makes clear, “I cannot lie to you and say that I already know which kind it is.” The traveler then places the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and asks, “is this a coincidence? Yun Gui, have you seen me before? You haven’t been hiding anything from me, right?”—the questioning shifts for the first time from “what was that call in the dream” to “who is Yun Gui himself,” pulling Yun Gui himself into the very center of this mystery of identity. Yun Gui answers truthfully: he acknowledges, “there is the word ‘gui’ in my name,” makes clear, “before tonight, I did not recognize you,” admits that what he knows is not more than what the traveler brought back from the dream, and says, “about you—I will not use your memory to deceive you, nor will I hide from you any clues I know.” As for “hiding anything from you,” he only says, “this relay station has its own old affairs, and I also have old affairs left from my many years of keeping the lamp,” without making an absolute statement. The traveler accepts this truthfulness, loosens his hand slightly but still hooks Yun Gui’s fingertips, saying, “I’m not trying to convict you, I’m just afraid that even you will suddenly become unfamiliar,” and proposes an agreement: “promise me, if you remember anything related to me, even if it is bad, you will tell me, all right?”—turning the coincidence between the word “gui” and Yun Gui’s name from an accusation into an agreement. Yun Gui truthfully agrees to this agreement, draws the boundary of “not stating a doubtful shadow as a conclusion,” and gives the next direction that can be checked—“when day breaks and the fog is thinner, I will bring the relay station’s old guest register for you to look at.” If the traveler accepts this truthfulness and brings the questioning back under the lamplight, the two of them, under the lamp, compare the pattern on the half piece of jade with the shallow pattern on the broken silver ring, and test again the resonance between the tongueless copper bell and the jade; or, after daybreak, they look through the old guest register together. This would move from “retreating back indoors, setting the fragments alongside one another and recording them, keeping night watch” into the substantive stage of “bringing the fragments close to one another under the lamp and identifying whom that line leads to.” This is a new situation explained by the events that have already occurred (the first awakening, the questioning, handing over tea, asking about sensations, the traveler seeking help, Yun Gui checking and discovering the fragments, pushing the jade to the palm, the traveler gripping the jade and giving a fragment, Yun Gui taking out the copper bell and folding the matter back under the lamplight, walking to the old well and prying out the silver ring, the traveler asking to return indoors, Yun Gui agreeing and setting the items alongside one another and recording them, agreeing to keep watch and remember on his behalf, the traveler lying down and adding the request to guard his dreams, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to wake him and confirm reality, the traveler closing his eyes and adding a final confirmation, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing and sitting guard, the traveler’s first outward dream murmuring after falling asleep, Yun Gui truthfully answering and reaffirming his presence, the traveler waking and reporting the word “gui,” Yun Gui truthfully responding and recording the word “gui,” the traveler placing the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and questioning him, Yun Gui truthfully answering and acknowledging his own old affairs, the traveler loosening his hand and asking for an agreement, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to the agreement and giving the checkable direction of the old guest register), rather than a jump to an unrelated plotline.

Yun Gui, have you seen me before? You haven’t been hiding anything from me, right?”—the questioning shifts for the first time from “what was that call in the dream” to “who is Yun Gui himself,” pulling Yun Gui himself into the very center of this mystery of identity. goal_tracking.underlying_goal: One possible deeper motive: Yun Gui is waiting on behalf of an old guest who has not returned for many years, and is therefore especially cautious about “leaving someone behind” and “someone waiting.” The call in the traveler’s dream and the character “Gui” happen also to be the question to which he himself has received no answer for many years. Now the traveler has again placed the character “Gui” alongside his name and asked, “Have you seen me before?” He is unwilling to give an answer he himself is not certain of, and he is also unwilling to let another traveler leave carrying false hope.
evidence: latent state anxiety: “When the traveler places the character “gui” beside his name and asks, “Have you seen me before?”, it cuts closer to him than in the previous turn—he has kept a lamp for someone who has not returned for many years, and understands best the seam between “someone is waiting” and “the person being waited for cannot come back.””
hidden_constraints: “In fact, in his heart he is also waiting for an old guest who has not returned for many years.”
assistant #25: "This relay station has its own old stories, and I have old stories left from my many years of keeping the lamp."
counter_evidence: Yun Gui’s aloofness and “being used to partings” may also simply be professional restraint, not necessarily related to some specific old visitor.
"Not lightly promising a route home" can also be explained solely by the world mechanism (those who ask too urgently cannot get out of Wuxia Pass), with no need for a deeper motive.
Yungui does not say everything about “what is being kept from you”; this may also simply be the lamp keeper’s usual sense of proportion, rather than being related to some old guest.
alternatives: Explanation 1: Yungui’s caution comes purely from reverence for the rules of the fog pass and the duties of a lamp keeper.
Explanation two: Yungui’s caution stems from not knowing the way home themself, and therefore being unable to give an answer.
Interpretation three: Yun Gui's caution is related to a certain old guest, but it is not necessarily “waiting”; it may also be guilt or an unfinished promise.

Yun Gui catches the fragment, repeats it word for word and confirms that “this is already a line,” then takes out a tongueless copper bell—which unexpectedly trembles when brought near the jade, providing the first verifiable physical response to the clue; at the same time, he agrees to the request to go together, but folds “accompanying” back into what can be done under the lamplight (search the relay station first: beneath the eaves, at the threshold, by the old well), and makes clear that “if the fog does not recede, we will not go out tonight.” The two walk to the old well beneath the eaves; the copper bell rings again, and Yun Gui pries a broken silver ring from a gap between the stones (its pattern seems faintly connectable to the jade’s, but a middle piece is missing). The traveler flashes on “a red umbrella, a hand wearing a silver ring” and takes the initiative to ask to return inside. Yun Gui immediately agrees, protects him as he crosses back under the corridor, helps him sit by the couch, wraps the copper bell in cloth and places it beside the lamp, and sets the new fragment alongside the others and records it. present: The traveler answers, “it has receded a little… but I’m still afraid,” asks Yun Gui, “can you stay here tonight,” hands over the right to safekeep the memory of “that red umbrella and silver ring—you’ll remember them for me, right,” and finally says, “if that person really is still waiting, I don’t want to forget him.” Yun Gui agrees to keep watch through the night and to remember on his behalf—he takes a low stool and sits guard beside the couch, puts the copper bell, silver ring, and white jade into a small wooden box without closing the lid, takes out an old booklet and writes down word by word: “Red umbrella. Rain. Bell sound. Wellside. Silver ring. After the traveler falls asleep, the first outward manifestation of dream murmuring occurs—in the dream he still clutches the corner of the quilt tightly, calls “Yun Gui… don’t go,” reports “there’s someone under the red umbrella, he is calling me… but I can’t hear what comes after. The bell rang again,” and asks after him, “Yun Gui, are you still there?”—this is precisely the first time Yun Gui’s dream anchor from the previous turn, “If you call, I will answer you,” is actually triggered. Yun Gui answers truthfully and draws the traveler back from the dream to the lamplight. The traveler suddenly opens his eyes, grips Yun Gui’s hand in return and says, “don’t let go,” and, in a waking state, reports for the first time, “the person under the red umbrella seemed to call my name, but I only heard the word ‘gui’… is it my name, or was he saying he wanted to go back?”—the memory fragment advances by one substantive step from “someone called me” to “what was called may be related to my name.” Yun Gui answers truthfully, “I’m here,” “I heard a little of it,” admits that he too only heard the word “gui,” writes the word “gui” into the old booklet, and makes clear, “I cannot lie to you and say that I already know which kind it is.” The traveler then places the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and asks, “is this a coincidence? Yun Gui, have you seen me before? You haven’t been hiding anything from me, right?”—the questioning shifts for the first time from “what was that call in the dream” to “who is Yun Gui himself,” pulling Yun Gui himself into the very center of this mystery of identity. Yun Gui answers truthfully: he acknowledges, “there is the word ‘gui’ in my name,” makes clear, “before tonight, I did not recognize you,” admits that what he knows is not more than what the traveler brought back from the dream, and says, “about you—I will not use your memory to deceive you, nor will I hide from you any clues I know.” As for “hiding anything from you,” he only says, “this relay station has its own old affairs, and I also have old affairs left from my many years of keeping the lamp,” without making an absolute statement. The traveler accepts this truthfulness, loosens his hand slightly but still hooks Yun Gui’s fingertips, saying, “I’m not trying to convict you, I’m just afraid that even you will suddenly become unfamiliar,” and proposes an agreement: “promise me, if you remember anything related to me, even if it is bad, you will tell me, all right?”—turning the coincidence between the word “gui” and Yun Gui’s name from an accusation into an agreement. Yun Gui truthfully agrees to this agreement, draws the boundary of “not stating a doubtful shadow as a conclusion,” and gives the next direction that can be checked—“when day breaks and the fog is thinner, I will bring the relay station’s old guest register for you to look at.” If the traveler accepts this truthfulness and brings the questioning back under the lamplight, the two of them, under the lamp, compare the pattern on the half piece of jade with the shallow pattern on the broken silver ring, and test again the resonance between the tongueless copper bell and the jade; or, after daybreak, they look through the old guest register together. This would move from “retreating back indoors, setting the fragments alongside one another and recording them, keeping night watch” into the substantive stage of “bringing the fragments close to one another under the lamp and identifying whom that line leads to.” This is a new situation explained by the events that have already occurred (the first awakening, the questioning, handing over tea, asking about sensations, the traveler seeking help, Yun Gui checking and discovering the fragments, pushing the jade to the palm, the traveler gripping the jade and giving a fragment, Yun Gui taking out the copper bell and folding the matter back under the lamplight, walking to the old well and prying out the silver ring, the traveler asking to return indoors, Yun Gui agreeing and setting the items alongside one another and recording them, agreeing to keep watch and remember on his behalf, the traveler lying down and adding the request to guard his dreams, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to wake him and confirm reality, the traveler closing his eyes and adding a final confirmation, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing and sitting guard, the traveler’s first outward dream murmuring after falling asleep, Yun Gui truthfully answering and reaffirming his presence, the traveler waking and reporting the word “gui,” Yun Gui truthfully responding and recording the word “gui,” the traveler placing the word “gui” alongside Yun Gui’s name and questioning him, Yun Gui truthfully answering and acknowledging his own old affairs, the traveler loosening his hand and asking for an agreement, Yun Gui truthfully agreeing to the agreement and giving the checkable direction of the old guest register), rather than a jump to an unrelated plotline.

No matter what else calls from the mist, do not answer first”; he led the traveler to recite sentence by sentence, “I am at Qixia Post Station,” “I am under the lamp,” “I do not pursue the voice in the mist,” pinning themself back beneath the lamp; finally he looked toward that dense white mass around the old well but did not take a step, only lifting the lamp a little higher, and said, “If that voice truly has a source, it will leave traces that can be distinguished under the lamp. There is no need to trade your soul for it,” and asked, “Now tell me: is the white jade still giving off heat? Is the heat growing stronger, or is it being pressed down by the lamp?”

plot_point: The traveler follows closely beside Yun Gui to the pillar in the east corridor, then suddenly presses a hand to the white jade at their chest and reports, “It’s heating up, as if toward the old well”—the white jade shows a physical directional response for the first time, and it points precisely toward the old well where the person with the red umbrella left years ago.

The traveler proactively triggers the safety valve jointly confirmed by both sides in the previous turn—“Yungui, call me back first”—and does not chase after it, but first calls on Yungui to stop things, returning the right of judgment to Yungui.

The traveler presses further, “Is this the road it recognized?” — directly linking the white jade’s physical indication to the unresolved question of “whether it recognizes a road,” requiring Yungui to answer truthfully between “admitting the jade is heating up” and “not therefore asserting where it leads.”

The fog by the old well curled slightly, like a water surface stepped on by someone; the silver ring sounded once, and from the fog came an extremely faint call of "return"—colliding with that night in the old register, and with the sound left behind when that person turned and left in the rain.

Yun Gui responds immediately: first raising the lamp, clasping the wrist, and pressing the pulse to confirm the traveler is present, calling softly, "Come back"; turning sideways to block the traveler's view toward the well mouth; refusing to make an absolute statement about "is he calling you, or calling me," and pointing out that "the fog is best at choosing words like this to call people"; pressing the white jade together with the traveler's hand against the traveler's chest, not letting it continue pulling toward the well; leading the traveler in reciting three sentences to pin themself back under the lamp; and at the end asking, "Is the white jade still heating up? Is the heat getting stronger, or being pressed down by the lamp?"
attention: Traveler: The panic is still at its highest point, but in this turn it is pinned down by a concrete physical signal—the white jade really is heating up, and it is pointing toward the old well. My first reaction is not to run after it, but to press my chest and call for him to bring me back first. Yet “Is this the path it recognized?” still has no answer, and “Why would you forget me?” still has no answer either.

Traveler: all their attention is pulled by the white jade growing warm—it points toward the old well, precisely the direction in which the red-umbrella person left back then. I both want to know immediately whether that is the road home and am afraid of being dragged back into that rain, so I first call for him to bring me back. Wanting to hear clearly and fearing hearing clearly, the two forces are still pulling.

Traveler: That sound of “Gui” in the fog happens to collide with his name again, and I cannot help asking, “Is he calling you, or me?” — I still remember that half-finished old matter too. If he answers truthfully and first calls me back, I will trust him more; if he takes the opening and says, “this is the road it recognized,” I will instead be afraid.

Yun Gui: his attention is more concretely placed on this traveler — the other party stays close beside him while walking up to the corridor pillar; when the white jade heats up, the first reaction is not to chase outside, but to call to him, “Call me back first.” This is the first practical use after handing the thing they fear losing most into his hands. He can receive it, and is willing to answer truthfully, without making promises he cannot fulfill just because he is being depended on.

Yun Gui: the white jade truly gives off heat under the lamp and points toward the old well, directly striking the old matter for which he has had no answer for many years—that unfinished half-sentence costs him another bit of mental effort compared with the previous turn. That call of “Gui” in the fog is too much like that night in the old register, too much like the sound left behind when that person turned and left in the rain, making his heart sink with it. That slight heaviness is pressed back into the lamp flame as usual, not letting the traveler notice.

Yun Gui: what he is watching for is not to let Baiyu’s heat be hastily taken as “the road it has recognized”—“Mist Pass is best at tangling similar words together; the more urgently you try to recognize them, the easier it is to recognize them wrongly”. Therefore he first agrees to stop when called, reiterates his presence, and narrows the next step down to what can be done under the lamp (only going as far as the corridor pillar, using the lamp to shine from a distance), holding the measure of “not hastily agreeing to any call from within the fog”.

The jointly significant point for both sides: that piece of white jade—the traveler sees it as the thing they most fear losing (possibly their own name), and now it is truly heating up and pointing toward the old well, becoming the first physical direction to appear in this line; Yungui sees it as something he can promise to accompany and safeguard, while it also happens to be the question to which he himself has found no answer for many years. Now it has again been gathered into the investigable direction of 'bring the lamp to illuminate the white jade and see whether it recognizes that old road.' It becomes the heaviest point in each of their hearts, yet neither has spoken it plainly.

goal_tracking.underlying_goal: One possible deeper motivation: Yungui is waiting on behalf of an old guest who has not returned for many years, and is therefore especially cautious about “leaving someone behind” and “someone waiting.” The call in the traveler’s dream and the character “gui” happen to be precisely the question to which he himself has had no answer for many years; now the white jade has truly grown warm and points toward the old well where the red-umbrella person left years ago, and in the fog the call of “gui” appears again. He neither wants to give an answer he himself is not sure of, nor wants to let yet another traveler leave with false hope.

counter_evidence: Yun Gui’s aloofness and “being used to partings” may also simply be professional restraint, not necessarily related to some specific old visitor.
"Not lightly promising a route home" can also be explained solely by the world mechanism (those who ask too urgently cannot get out of Wuxia Pass), with no need for a deeper motive.
Yungui does not say everything about “what is being kept from you”; this may also simply be the lamp keeper’s usual sense of proportion, rather than being related to some old guest.
alternatives: Explanation 1: Yungui’s caution comes purely from reverence for the rules of the fog pass and the duties of a lamp keeper.

Don’t let me chase into the fog alone.” Yun Gui truthfully agrees to accompany him, holds the boundary of “only as far as the lamplight reaches,” sets in advance a boundary regarding calls from within the fog, and leads the traveler to get up and walk toward the east corridor. present: The traveler stays close to Yun Gui as they reach the corridor pillar; the white jade suddenly heats up and points toward the old well.
